lines.note: Nagekomi/nagekomu means putting something in by throwing it. The circumflex in the abbreviated past principal part is retained as printed, not harmonized with other -comi entries.
The example describes treating a holy man harshly before throwing him into snow. Sennin is the object of the action; the final yuqino modifies the snow-filled hole on the following row.

The hole is one in which snow has accumulated; naguecomi supplies the act of throwing the man into it. The following abbreviated part reference belongs with the citation label on the next row, not with the Japanese example.

runs.text: Tratando muito mal ao ſancto o me

lines.note: The roman citation label precedes the Portuguese translation, which calls the victim a saint. The final me begins meterão on the following physical line; no terminal hyphen is supplied where the scan shows none.

runs.text: terão em hũa coua chea de neue.

lines.note: Completes meterão: they put him into a pit full of snow. The printed tilde is over the u in hũa; chea and neue retain the historical spellings.
Nagekoshi describes throwing something over another object. The oita principal part is consistent with the dictionary's historical s-verb forms; the Portuguese noun is physically divided cou- / ſa.
Completes the object and specifies the trajectory: one thing is thrown over another. This short continuation remains a separate row rather than being attached to the next headword.
Nagekube means throwing something into a fire. The phrase no fogo continues onto the next row, where a quoted example explains the entry.
The example begins 'immediately, this head ... into the fire'. Fini is hi ni, with the historical f spelling; nague continues directly into cubetaruni on the next row without a printed hyphen.

Completes nagekubetaru ni and states that the head sprang out of the fire. The vodoriide- form is supported by the Portuguese description of jumping out, rather than being treated as a malformed modern spelling.

runs.text: Lib. 24. Logo em botãdo esta ca-

lines.note: The citation gives book 24, followed by 'as soon as this head was thrown'. Botãdo is the preferred reading of the abraded word: the nasal abbreviation and surviving letters support it, but the central types remain damaged. The source label is kept roman.

runs.text: beça no fogo, ſahio ſaltando de dentro do fogo.

lines.note: Completes cabeça and says that it came leaping out of the fire. The tall letter in ſahio is read as h, consistent with the visible italic form and the verb 'came out'; OCR ſabio would misidentify the word.
Nagedashi means throwing something out. The final fo- belongs to fora below, and aita is the dictionary's abbreviated historical past form, not an instruction to modernize the verb.
The first gloss specifies throwing outside a doorway. Ashi wo begins a separate example about stretching out the legs, with nagedasu divided across the row boundary.
Completes ashi wo nagedasu, extending the legs or feet outward. The Portuguese infinitive Estender and the doubled-vowel pees are retained in their printed spelling.
Completes pera fora, 'outward', in the explanation of stretching the legs. The short row belongs to the preceding example rather than the next headword.
Nageidashi is referred back to nagedashi by Idem. The additional i is a visible part of this alternative verb form and is not removed to match the previous spelling.
Nage no nasake is explained as affection or hospitality that is only pretended. The Portuguese adjective begins fin- and continues below; agaſalhado is retained as the printed form.

runs.text: gido, ou feito ſoomente no exterior.

lines.note: Completes fingido and contrasts outward appearance with genuine affection. The damaged first word is read gido, not OCR gilo; feito is supported by the surviving types. The terminal P. is the upright poetry label.

Nageki, nageku, nageita means grieving or feeling great concern. The diagonal damage crosses the headword, but its surviving letters, the following example, and the supplied NINJAL entry support Nagueqi. The two provisional IDs c1-l020 and c1-l021 represented this same physical row; its text is retained here once. Lexical aid used for these page reviews: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset).

Cuidados completes 'have great cares'; the example go-shoo wo nageku concerns anxiety about the life to come. The omitted left-hand word has been restored to this existing row. Its ending is partly obscured by diagonal damage, so cuidados remains a qualified reading rather than entirely clear type.

runs.text: girſe, & moſtrarſe ſolicito pollas couſas da

lines.note: Completes afligir-se and explains showing solicitude for matters of salvation. Moſtrarſe is partly abraded but matches the visible surviving sequence and the Portuguese construction, unlike OCR moſtearſe.
Salvação completes the religious gloss of concern for the next life. The word remains a separate physical continuation and is not joined to the noun entry below.
Nageki is the noun 'grief' or 'care', distinct from the inflected verb just above. The final Nague- starts the phrase nageki ni shizumu on the following row.
Nageki ni shizumu literally evokes sinking in sorrow, rendered as being full of sadness. Xizzumu is retained with its printed doubled z; the Portuguese list continues below.
Aflição completes the pair 'sadness and affliction'. The damaged letter is the l of aflição rather than the OCR's t, as confirmed by the surrounding Portuguese gloss.

Nageki kanashimi combines grieving and sorrowing. The damaged initial letter is N, not OCR X; the phrase and supplied NINJAL headword corroborate Nagueqi canaximi. The caron over the abbreviated past form is retained.

Completes the definition as grieving and becoming very sad. Diagonal abrasion crosses entristecerſe; the surviving beginning and ending support this reading, replacing the nonsensical OCR entrearerſe.
Nagetsuke is making something strike or stick by throwing it. The first principal-part ending reads uru, not OCR aru, matching the visible letters and the verb's historical lower-bigrade pattern.

runs.text: couſa, ou arremeſar algũa couſa a outra, como

lines.note: Continues the explanation as throwing one thing at another. The middle of arremeſar is damaged by the diagonal defect; surviving letters and the parallel verb in nearby entries support the chosen reading.
The example is mud or clay thrown against a wall. Barro, with final o and doubled r, is visible rather than OCR barre; the grave accent belongs to à.
Nageuchi, nageutsu, nageutta means throwing something. The roman v is clear in the headword, correcting Nagueychi; algũa is partly crossed by damage but remains identifiable in the Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met. Deixar, ou largar total-

lines.note: A figurative sense follows: abandoning or relinquishing something completely. Total- is damaged near the right edge but is supported by surviving letters and mente below; the whole Portuguese segment is italic, not alternating stray roman fragments.
Completes totalmente and begins an example about service to God. Both long-o marks in gofôcô are visibly circumflexes, correcting the OCR carons without modernizing the Japanese spelling.
The example means relinquishing all things for God's service. Naguevtçu is preserved as the printed finite verb, while the Portuguese por connects with ſeruiço on the next row.
Completes 'for the service of God'. The Portuguese spelling Deos is retained independently of Deusno in the Japanese example.
The noun nageuchi denotes a throw or cast. Qide is Japanese ki de, 'with a stick', and its final e belongs to the roman example rather than to the italic gloss.
Ki de nageuchi suru is explained as throwing with a stick. The Portuguese reads com, not OCR cont; a second construction starts with Qi- at the right edge.
Completes ki wo nageuchi ni suru and assigns it the same meaning. The object marker uo belongs to the divided Qi- from the previous row, not to an independent headword.
Nageoroshi is throwing from above downward. The printed vo sequence is preserved in the headword rather than rewritten to modern romanization.
Completes the direction 'downward'. Pera is the historical Portuguese form here and is not changed to para.
Nageotoshi describes throwing something so that it falls or is knocked down. The Portuguese gerund derrubando is divided after der- at the line edge.
Completes derrubando, specifying the result of the throwing action. This is a genuine one-word continuation, not redundant material.

runs.text: Paos que ſe prègão ſobre os Nuquis,

lines.note: Nageshi are timbers fastened above the nuki crosspieces. Nuquis is a Japanese architectural term embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is flagged for whole-word typeface review; the printed grave in prègão is retained.

runs.text: ou traueßas das columnas pera mais fortalecer,

lines.note: The Portuguese further describes those crosspieces as traversing the columns and strengthening the building. The historical double-s ligature in traueßas is kept, as is the printed comma after fortalecer.
Completes the purpose clause: strengthening the building. The short continuation is kept separate from the following verb entry.

Nagi, nagu, naida concerns the wind ceasing and the waves becoming still. Ceßar corrects the garbled OCR Coßſar; the abbreviated plural ending in ſoſegarẽ belongs with as ondas at the top of column 2.
Continues the entry from column 1 and gives kaze ga naida, 'the wind fell calm'. Cajega uses the dictionary's historical spelling of kaze; it is not a new headword.
Completes Encalmou o vento, the wind becoming calm. The physical column transition has not interrupted the entry's sense.
The noun nagi denotes calm or serenity of the weather. The final tem- is the first part of tempo, continued on the next row.

runs.text: po quando não venta, & eſtà o mar quieto. Vt,

lines.note: Specifies weather without wind and with a quiet sea. The scan supports the separate article in eſtà o mar and the masculine quieto, correcting the fused OCR eſtào and final quieta.
Fune ni noru tame ni yoi nagi ja means that the calm is suitable for taking a boat. The grave printed over the first u in Fùneni is retained despite the ordinary word fune not requiring a long vowel.

runs.text: bom tempo, ou quieto pera ſe embarcar.

lines.note: The translation describes good, calm weather for embarking. Quieto characterizes the weather rather than an instruction that the passenger should remain quiet.
This separate nagi verb concerns cutting with a halberd or sickle. Its identical principal parts do not make it a continuation of the calm-weather entry.
The cutting motion is a sweeping or backhand stroke. A narrative example begins with Benkei and his opponent's knee region; the latter phrase continues on the next row.

Continues the knee-level action: a breeze is raised by the sweep, followed by the mimetic sarari-sarari. Nai is the first part of naida; the right rule is visible and no extra terminal material is supplied.

Da completes naida. The roman source label Toſ. precedes a Portuguese rendering in which Benquei makes wind with the weapon; Benquei is a name embedded in Portuguese and is flagged for typeface review.

runs.text: Naguinata por perto dos joelhos com eſtrondo

lines.note: The weapon passes near the knees with a rushing sound. Naguinata is embedded in the Portuguese explanation, unlike its ordinary headword later on this page, and is therefore included among the whole-word typeface terms.

The narrative says that he cut the opponent's legs; cortara is preferred over OCR cortata, although the second r is badly abraded. A new example, kusa wo nagu, illustrates cutting grass rather than a combat action.
The alternative ine wo nagu means cutting rice plants. The Latin l, means 'or'; the Portuguese has the visible doubled r in arroz, correcting OCR aroz.
Adds that the cut material is left in the field. The historical attached pronoun in deixandoo is retained rather than modernized with a hyphen.

Nagifuse means felling by a sweeping cut. The printed principal part ſuru is retained even though uru might look more regular beside many neighboring entries; the supplied NINJAL entry independently records suru here.
Completes derrubar por terra, knocking to the ground. The example begins with the naginata as instrument and mucǒ describing enemies facing the attacker.
Completes the example by saying that five enemies were cut down. Naguifuxe is supported by the surviving letters and the headword, replacing OCR nazuiruxe; Feiq. is the roman citation label.
Gives book 2 of the cited source and begins the translation, 'cutting and bringing down with the ...'. The book reference belongs to the italic apparatus, not to the Japanese citation label above.

runs.text: Naguinata cinco inimigos que eſtauão de frõ-

lines.note: The translation specifies five enemies facing the attacker. Cinco is visible, not OCR cino. The damaged verb is read eſtauão from the surviving ending and past-tense context; its medial u remains uncertain. Naguinata is an embedded Japanese term.
Completes de fronte and adds the alternative that the enemies were coming to meet the attacker. The verb vinhão retains its historical nasal spelling.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de alabarda que tem

lines.note: Naginata is defined by comparison with a kind of halberd. Maneira is clear enough to correct OCR maneita; the precise blade description continues below.

runs.text: o ferro como de fouce roçadoura.

lines.note: Describes the metal blade as resembling that of a clearing sickle. This comparative historical description is retained without substituting a modern weapon classification.
Nagisa is the shore where waves break. The headword's long ſ and the Portuguese spelling Praya are preserved.
Nagoshi no harai is located by the dictionary on the last day of the sixth lunar month. The gloss gives a calendrical identification rather than a full account of the purification observance.
Nagusame is transitive here: comforting or cheering another person. Its gloss contrasts with the reflexive recreation given under nagusami below.
Kokoro wo nagusamuru means comforting or refreshing the heart. The historical -muru form belongs to the verb just defined and is not replaced by modern -meru.
Completes the explanation as gladdening the heart. The Portuguese object is the same kokoro expressed in the Japanese example.
Nagusami is the intransitive or self-directed counterpart, taking comfort or recreation. The caron in the abbreviated past principal part is visible and retained.
This is the noun 'recreation' or 'diversion', not a duplicate of the preceding inflected verb. Its brief gloss is a complete entry on one physical line.
Nai expresses nonexistence or absence. The dictionary labels it a defective verb; that historical grammatical classification is preserved rather than replaced with a modern analysis.

runs.text: Fazer, ou torcer com a mão cor-

lines.note: A different nai entry concerns twisting cord by hand. The long-vowel principal parts belong to this verb and must not be confused with the preceding negative nai.
Completes cordas and illustrates nawa wo noo, twisting a rope. The caron in nǒ agrees with the form printed in the entry, without expanding the canonical text.

Naikan is paraphrased as inward consideration and equated with naisan. The Portuguese specifies private calculation on the next row; the tilde in cãgayuru is an abbreviation and is not expanded in transcription.
Completes 'making the accounts with oneself', meaning calculation carried out privately. Conſigo and meſmo retain their visible long-s forms.

Naikoku is glossed as 'just now', with sunawachi toki as the Japanese explanation. The scan supports Naicocu and toqi, correcting OCR Naiencu and roqi; the supplied NINJAL entry corroborates the headword identification.
Naidan is secret consultation, paraphrased as naishoo no dankoo. The circumflex in Naixôno and caron in dancǒ are separate visible choices, not a uniform accent convention to impose on the line.

runs.text: Humliuro que trata das couſas da ſal

lines.note: Naiden is described as a book concerning religious salvation. Humliuro retains the close printed spacing; ſal is the first part of ſaluação, continued without a visible hyphen.

Completes the reference to the salvation of the 'gentiles', the missionaries' wording for the non-Christian religious setting. The note identifies the historical perspective without adopting it as a modern description.
Naihyoo is another term for secret consultation, paraphrased as hisokana dankoo. The headword's fiǒ sequence and caron are preserved rather than collapsed to the distinct naifoo entry below.
Naihoo, equated with uchikata, denotes a wife or married woman. The Portuguese Molher is the printed historical spelling, not an OCR error requiring modern mulher.

runs.text: Riquezas, ou bẽs que hum tem ſem

lines.note: Naifuku denotes wealth or possessions that a person has without displaying them. The tilde in bẽs abbreviates the nasal consonant and is not expanded.
Completes the contrast between inward wealth and outward appearance. The example begins naifuku shita hito, with hito divided fi- / to across the row boundary.

runs.text: Homem que està rico, mas não o parece

lines.note: Completes hito and translates it as a man who is wealthy but does not appear so. The grave in està is retained independently of other accent placements on the page.
'Outwardly' completes the description of concealed prosperity. It closes the naifuku example before the next headword begins.
Naigaku is explained by uchi manabu, studying or rehearsing privately. The Portuguese offers rehearsal and study as related explanations rather than defining a particular school or institution.

runs.text: eſtudo, & exercicio de letras: que ſe faz em

lines.note: Continues with study and literary exercise undertaken at home. The place phrase em caſa is split over this and the following physical row. The second pass distinguishes a colon after letras from the OCR comma.

runs.text: caſa primeiro que ſaya em publico.

lines.note: Completes the idea of practice at home before appearing in public. The line is visibly a continuation and its indentation has been corrected; it is not an independent entry.
